tip: Dry hop warm for flavour, cold for clean extraction. Two to three days of contact is usually enough before grassy notes creep in.
Store hop pellets cold, dark and oxygen-free. Once a foil pack is opened, flush it with CO2 and reseal before it goes back in the freezer.
Measure mash pH at room temperature, about ten minutes after dough-in. Aim for 5.2 to 5.6 and adjust next brew, not mid-mash.
Do not rush a lager off its yeast. A diacetyl rest near 16 to 18 °C as fermentation finishes saves weeks of buttery regret.
Underpitching costs more than yeast. Pitch about 0.75 million cells per ml per degree Plato for ales and roughly double for lagers.
Oxygenate cold wort, never hot. Hot-side aeration stales flavour, while cold wort needs oxygen for healthy yeast growth.
Clean draught lines every two weeks at minimum. A dirty line can make a perfect beer taste stale, sour or buttery at the tap.
Serve lagers colder than ales. Pouring a stout at fridge temperature hides the roast and chocolate you paid to brew.
Hoppy beer fades fastest. Keep IPA cold from tank to tap, because Indian summer heat ages it weeks in a few days.
Take original and final gravity on every batch and write them down. ABV is (OG minus FG) times 131.25. Excise will ask.
Test your water before you change a recipe. Borewell water can swing in hardness between seasons and shift every beer you make.
Cold crash slowly if you can. A sudden drop pulls in air through the airlock and adds oxygen right before packaging.
Number every keg and log where it goes. Small breweries lose more money in missing kegs than in spilt beer.
Taste in the same order every time: look, smell, sip, then breathe out through your nose. Most flavour arrives on the exhale.
Name the off-flavour before you fix it. Green apple, butter and cooked corn each point to a different step in your process.
Before you change a flagship recipe, run a triangle test. If tasters cannot pick the odd glass out, keep the cheaper option.
Recalculate bitterness from the alpha on this season's certificate of analysis, never last year's figure. Low-alpha German hops give fewer IBUs.
If your house Pilsner relies on Saaz, Tettnanger or Mittelfrüh, order early this season and ask whether the stock is 2025 or 2026 crop.
Buy only as many hops as your freezer holds. A vacuum pack at around -18 °C keeps; a warm godown ruins any bargain.
Trial a new hop in a single-hop pale ale beside a control beer brewed with a hop you already know well.
HPA suggests Luna at 1 to 2 g/L in a late whirlpool for citrus and 4 to 10 g/L as a dry hop.
When dry hopping with HyperBoost, Yakima Chief Hops advises oil for only 25 to 50% of the charge, with pellets making up the rest.
Mix a flowable whirlpool extract such as Incognito with a little hot wort before adding it, so it disperses evenly.
Grape-skin thiol precursors like Phantasm only release aroma with a thiol-releasing yeast. Dose in the whirlpool, around 6 g/L to start.
Cryo Fresh pellets are for dry hopping only. Use CO2 extract or T90 pellets when you need bitterness in the kettle.
Never halve a pellet weight by rule of thumb when switching to a concentrate. Recalculate alpha and oil, then brew a small trial first.
Alcohol-free beer grew 8% by volume worldwide in 2025. A well-made one on your tap list is worth the effort.
With a maltose-negative yeast, pasteurise every pack. The maltose left behind will feed any spoilage organism that gets in.
Dealcoholisation strips esters along with the ethanol. Plan your hop aroma for after the process rather than before it.
FSSAI caps a non-alcoholic counterpart at 0.5% ABV. A hydrometer cannot measure that accurately, so budget for proper alcohol testing.
Trial a new yeast as a split batch: same wort, two fermenters, one change. Taste blind at packaging and four weeks later.
Diastatic yeast can keep fermenting in the can until it gushes. Ask your supplier for the STA1 result before you pitch a saison strain.
Check viability when imported yeast arrives after a hot courier run. A trial on tired yeast tells you about the courier, not the strain.
Before ordering an engineered yeast for an Indian brewery, get your licensing adviser to confirm the current position on GM cultures in writing.
Fermentation makes about 4 kg of CO2 per hectolitre of 5% beer. Multiply by your annual volume before any vendor quotes a recovery unit.
Payback is capital cost divided by yearly savings after running costs. Use your own CO2 and power prices, never the brochure's.
Make sure the hot side of your wort cooler fills the hot liquor tank for the next brew. That heat is already paid for.
Karnataka now taxes beer by its alcohol content. Rerun your price list for every ABV before you finalise a recipe for that market.
Cans and glass both ran short in India within a year. Line up a second packaging supplier before you print a single label.
